modules.title: 1 · Why OLS fails
modules.summary: Endogeneity from omitted variables and simultaneity makes OLS biased and inconsistent.

stages.title: The exogeneity assumption
stages.html:
What OLS quietly assumes

Write the model as

y = β₀ + β₁·x + ε

OLS gives a consistent, unbiased estimate of β₁ only if the regressor is exogenous: the error term ε must be uncorrelated with x, written Cov(x, ε) = 0. Intuitively, everything we left out of the model (bundled into ε) must not move together with x.

When instead Cov(x, ε) ≠ 0 we say x is endogenous. OLS then attributes to x variation that really belongs to ε, and β̂₁ is pulled away from the truth.

Key idea. OLS regresses y on all the comovement between x and y. If part of that comovement runs through ε, OLS cannot tell the causal part from the contaminated part — and the bias does not shrink as n → ∞.

Two classic ways endogeneity arises

  • Omitted variables. A confounder u drives both x and y. Leaving u out dumps it into ε, so x and ε share u.
  • Simultaneity / reverse causality. y also feeds back into x (price ↔ quantity, police ↔ crime), so x responds to the same shocks as y.

stages.title: The sign and size of the bias
stages.html:
How big is the OLS bias?

Suppose the true structural model has a confounder u that we cannot observe:

x = π·u + v, y = β₀ + β₁·x + γ·u + η

Because u appears in both equations, x carries information about u, and u sits inside the regression error ε = γ·u + η. The asymptotic OLS bias is

plim β̂₁ = β₁ + γ · Cov(x,u)/Var(x)

So the bias has the sign of γ·π (the product of how u affects y and how u affects x). If both effects are positive, OLS overstates β₁; if they have opposite signs it understates it.

Key idea. More data sharpens a wrong answer: the standard error shrinks around a biased point. Precision is not the same as correctness.

This is why we need a new strategy. We cannot fix endogeneity by collecting more rows — we need extra information in the form of an instrument, the subject of Module 2.

stages.title: Watch OLS miss the truth
stages.note: True β₁ = 2. A hidden confounder u raises both x and y, so OLS overshoots — and tightening n does not help.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def ols_slope(n):
    u = rng.normal(0,1,n)                # hidden confounder
    x = 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)        # u drives x
    y = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)# u also drives y (true beta1=2)
    return sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit().params[1]

ns = [50,100,200,500,1000,2000]
est = [ols_slope(n) for n in ns]
for n,b in zip(ns,est):
    print(f'n={n:5d}   OLS beta1_hat = {b:.3f}   (true = 2.000)')

plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.axhline(2,color='#c9c6ac',ls='--',lw=2,label='true beta1 = 2')
plt.plot(ns,est,'o-',color='#da9100',lw=2,label='OLS estimate')
plt.xlabel('sample size n'); plt.ylabel('beta1_hat')
plt.title(f'OLS converges to {est[-1]:.2f}, not 2  (inconsistent)')
plt.legend()

stages.title: Confounding slider
stages.note: γ controls how strongly the hidden u also pushes y. At γ = 0 there is no confounding and OLS is fine; crank it up and the estimate drifts away from the true 2.

params.name: gamma
params.label: Confounder strength γ (effect of u on y)

stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n=800
u = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y = 1 + 2*x + {{gamma}}*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
b = res.params[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(x,y,s=10,color='#da9100',alpha=.4)
xs=np.linspace(x.min(),x.max(),50)
plt.plot(xs,res.params[0]+b*xs,color='#c9c6ac',lw=2,label='OLS fit')
plt.plot(xs,res.params[0]+2*xs,color='#af983f',lw=2,ls='--',label='true slope=2')
plt.legend(); plt.title(f'gamma={{gamma}}  ->  OLS beta1_hat = {b:.2f}  (bias {b-2:+.2f})')

stages.title: Check: source of the bias
stages.prompt: An unobserved variable raises both schooling x and wages y. We regress wages on schooling by OLS. What happens as the sample grows very large?
choices: The estimate converges to the true return to schooling
The estimate stays biased; only its standard error shrinks
The bias grows without bound
OLS becomes unbiased once n > 1000
stages.hint: Endogeneity is about consistency, not sampling noise.
stages.explain: Omitted-variable bias does not vanish with n. The point estimate converges to a wrong number while its SE shrinks around that wrong number — precise but inconsistent.

stages.title: Check: sign of the bias
stages.prompt: In x = π·u + v and y = β₁·x + γ·u + η, suppose γ > 0 and π > 0. OLS will tend to…
choices: overstate β₁
understate β₁
estimate β₁ exactly
give a negative β̂₁ regardless
stages.hint: The asymptotic bias has the sign of γ·π.
stages.explain: With γ·π > 0 the omitted u creates positive comovement between x and the error, so OLS attributes extra positive slope to x and overstates β₁.

modules.title: 2 · Instruments
modules.summary: A valid instrument is relevant (moves x) and excluded (affects y only through x).

stages.title: What is an instrument?
stages.html:
Borrowing clean variation

An instrument z is a variable that nudges the endogenous regressor x but is otherwise unrelated to the outcome's error. If we can isolate the part of x that moves because of z, that part is clean — uncontaminated by the confounder — and we can use it to estimate β₁ honestly.

A valid instrument must satisfy two conditions:

  • Relevance. z actually shifts x: Cov(z, x) ≠ 0. This is testable — you can see it in the data (Module 4's first-stage F).
  • Exclusion (exogeneity). z affects y only through x, and is uncorrelated with the error: Cov(z, ε) = 0. This is an assumption — it generally cannot be proven from data and must be argued from how the world works.
Key idea. z → x → y, with no arrow from z directly to y and no back-door from z to a confounder. The instrument's only path to the outcome runs through x.

stages.title: Why both conditions are indispensable
stages.html:
Break either leg and IV collapses

The IV estimand can be written as a ratio of covariances:

β₁ = Cov(z, y) / Cov(z, x)

Read the two requirements straight off this formula:

  • If relevance fails, Cov(z,x) ≈ 0 and we are dividing by (almost) zero — the estimator explodes and becomes wildly imprecise. This is the weak-instrument problem.
  • If exclusion fails, z sneaks into the numerator through its own correlation with ε, and Cov(z,y) no longer reflects only the z→x→y path. The estimate is biased — often worse than OLS.

Classic examples of plausible instruments:

  • Quarter of birth as an instrument for years of schooling (compulsory-schooling laws), for the return to education.
  • Distance to the nearest college as an instrument for college attendance.
  • Rainfall as an instrument for crop output / income in conflict studies.
Key idea. Relevance is checkable in your data; exclusion is a story you must defend. Reviewers attack the exclusion restriction, so make the argument explicit.

stages.title: See relevance vs exclusion in the data
stages.note: We can SEE relevance (z correlated with x). We assume exclusion (z uncorrelated with the structural error u). The plots make the difference concrete.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n=600
u = rng.normal(0,1,n)                 # confounder (unobserved error component)
z = rng.normal(0,1,n)                 # instrument
x = 1.2*z + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n) # z is RELEVANT for x
y = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n) # z enters y only through x (EXCLUSION holds)

print('corr(z, x)  =', round(np.corrcoef(z,x)[0,1], 3), ' <- relevance: should be far from 0')
print('corr(z, u)  =', round(np.corrcoef(z,u)[0,1], 3), ' <- exclusion: should be ~ 0')
print('corr(x, u)  =', round(np.corrcoef(x,u)[0,1], 3), ' <- x IS endogenous (nonzero)')

fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.7))
ax[0].scatter(z,x,s=8,color='#da9100',alpha=.4); ax[0].set_title('z vs x (relevant)'); ax[0].set_xlabel('z'); ax[0].set_ylabel('x')
ax[1].scatter(z,u,s=8,color='#c9c6ac',alpha=.4); ax[1].set_title('z vs u (excluded ~0)'); ax[1].set_xlabel('z'); ax[1].set_ylabel('u')
fig.tight_layout()

stages.title: Relevance slider
stages.note: Slide the first-stage coefficient π (how strongly z moves x). Near 0 the instrument is irrelevant; the printed correlation tells you whether IV has anything to work with.

params.name: pi
params.label: Instrument relevance π (effect of z on x)

stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); n=600
u=rng.normal(0,1,n); z=rng.normal(0,1,n)
x={{pi}}*z + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
r=np.corrcoef(z,x)[0,1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(z,x,s=10,color='#da9100',alpha=.45)
xs=np.linspace(z.min(),z.max(),50)
plt.plot(xs,{{pi}}*xs,color='#c9c6ac',lw=2)
plt.xlabel('instrument z'); plt.ylabel('regressor x')
plt.title(f'pi={{pi}}   corr(z,x) = {r:.2f}'+('   (weak!)' if abs(r)<0.15 else ''))

stages.title: Check: which property is testable?
stages.prompt: Which of the two IV conditions can you directly check from the observed data?
choices: Exclusion, by regressing y on z
Relevance, by checking that z is correlated with x
Both are fully testable
Neither can ever be examined
stages.hint: One condition involves the unobservable error.
stages.explain: Relevance (Cov(z,x) ≠ 0) is observable and testable via the first stage. Exclusion involves the unobservable error ε and must be argued from theory, not proven from data.

stages.title: Check: a broken instrument
stages.prompt: A proposed instrument z is strongly correlated with x but ALSO has its own direct effect on y. Using it in IV will…
choices: still give a consistent estimate of β₁
violate exclusion and generally yield a biased estimate
only inflate the standard errors
be fine as long as the first-stage F is large
stages.hint: z must affect y ONLY through x.
stages.explain: A direct z→y path violates the exclusion restriction, contaminating Cov(z,y). A huge first-stage F does not rescue an invalid instrument — it can make the bias more precise.

stages.title: Significant first stage ⇒ good instrument?
stages.prompt: You just saw that relevance is the one IV condition you can check in the data via the first stage. Claim: once the first-stage coefficient on z is statistically significant (t > 1.96), the instrument is strong enough to trust 2SLS.
stages.hint: Significance answers a different question (is the coefficient distinguishable from zero?) than strength (does z move x enough to divide by safely?).
stages.explain: This is the significance≠strength trap, the classic weak-instrument error. A first-stage t can clear 1.96 while the instrument is still weak: in 2SLS, strength is graded by the first-stage F on the excluded instruments (rule of thumb F ≳ 10), not by whether the coefficient beats zero. A barely-significant, low-F instrument biases 2SLS back toward OLS and wrecks the standard errors. Boundary: significance is necessary-ish but never sufficient — only a large first-stage F certifies strength.

stages.title: What makes an instrument valid?
stages.prompt: Z is a candidate instrument for an endogenous x. Select all that apply: which conditions MUST hold for Z to be a valid instrument?
choices: Relevance: Z is correlated with x (Cov(z,x) ≠ 0)
Exclusion: Z affects y only through x
Exogeneity: Z is uncorrelated with the structural error ε
Z has a statistically significant first-stage coefficient
Z is normally distributed
stages.hint: Two of these are the actual requirements you saw split into 'checkable' vs 'must be argued'; the others are properties students wrongly bolt on.
stages.explain: This bundles the validity conditions: relevance + exclusion + exogeneity. The strong distractor is 'significant first-stage coefficient' — that is the significance≠strength trap; significance is neither necessary nor sufficient, and a significant first stage can still be a weak (low-F) instrument. Normality of Z is never required — IV/2SLS makes no distributional assumption on the instrument. Boundary: relevance is the only one you can test from data; exclusion and exogeneity are arguments you must defend, not p-values you can read off.

modules.title: 3 · Two-Stage Least Squares
modules.summary: Project x on the instruments, then regress y on the fitted x to recover a consistent β₁.

stages.title: The two stages
stages.html:
2SLS in two moves

Two-Stage Least Squares operationalises the instrument idea:

  • First stage. Regress the endogenous x on the instrument(s) z (and any exogenous controls):
    x = π₀ + π₁·z + v. Keep the fitted values x̂. These are the part of x predicted by z — the clean, exogenous slice.
  • Second stage. Regress y on x̂ instead of x:
    y = β₀ + β₁·x̂ + error. Because x̂ is built only from z, it is uncorrelated with the confounder, so β̂₁ is consistent.
Key idea. x̂ strips out the contaminated variation in x and keeps only the variation z explains. Regressing on x̂ is like running the experiment z would have run for you.

With one endogenous regressor and one instrument the model is just-identified and 2SLS equals the simple IV ratio Cov(z,y)/Cov(z,x). With more instruments than endogenous regressors it is over-identified (Module 4).

stages.title: Do it in one call — and mind the SEs
stages.html:
Use a built-in estimator

You can run the two regressions by hand, but doing the second stage manually with sm.OLS(y, x̂) produces wrong standard errors: it ignores that x̂ is estimated, not observed. Use a dedicated estimator that corrects for this:

IV2SLS(endog, exog, instrument).fit()

The statsmodels signature (from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm) is:

  • endog = y
  • exog = the regressors in the structural equation — the constant and the endogenous x (plus any exogenous controls)
  • instrument = the constant and the instrument z (plus the same exogenous controls, which instrument themselves)

Build both design matrices with sm.add_constant. The point estimate matches the manual two-stage fit, but the reported SEs are now correct.

Key idea. Manual two-stage = right coefficient, wrong SE. IV2SLS = right coefficient and right SE.

stages.title: OLS bias vs consistent 2SLS
stages.note: Same data, three estimators. OLS is pulled up by the confounder; the hand-built two-stage and IV2SLS both land near the true β₁ = 2. Note the manual second stage prints a WRONG SE.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000
u = rng.normal(0,1,n)                 # confounder
z = rng.normal(0,1,n)                 # instrument
x = 1.2*z + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n) # endogenous (shares u with y)
y = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n) # true beta1 = 2

# OLS (biased)
ols = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
# Manual two-stage: project x on z, then regress y on x-hat
xhat = sm.OLS(x, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fittedvalues
man  = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(xhat)).fit()
# Proper IV2SLS (correct SEs)
exog = sm.add_constant(x); instr = sm.add_constant(z)
iv   = IV2SLS(y, exog, instr).fit()

print(f'true beta1            = 2.000')
print(f'OLS    beta1_hat      = {ols.params[1]:.3f}   SE {ols.bse[1]:.3f}  (biased up)')
print(f'manual 2-stage beta1  = {man.params[1]:.3f}   (SE here is WRONG: {man.bse[1]:.3f})')
print(f'IV2SLS beta1_hat      = {iv.params[1]:.3f}   SE {iv.bse[1]:.3f}  (consistent, correct SE)')

plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
labels=['OLS','IV2SLS']; vals=[ols.params[1],iv.params[1]]; errs=[ols.bse[1],iv.bse[1]]
plt.bar(labels,vals,yerr=errs,capsize=6,color=['#c9c6ac','#da9100'])
plt.axhline(2,color='#af983f',ls='--',lw=2,label='true = 2'); plt.legend()
plt.title(f'OLS {ols.params[1]:.2f}  vs  2SLS {iv.params[1]:.2f}')

stages.title: Confounding slider: OLS drifts, 2SLS holds
stages.note: Increase γ (effect of the confounder on y). OLS marches away from 2; as long as the instrument stays valid, 2SLS stays anchored near the truth.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000
u=rng.normal(0,1,n); z=rng.normal(0,1,n)
x=1.2*z+1.0*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
y=1+2*x+{{gamma}}*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
ols=sm.OLS(y,sm.add_constant(x)).fit().params[1]
iv =IV2SLS(y,sm.add_constant(x),sm.add_constant(z)).fit().params[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.bar(['OLS','2SLS'],[ols,iv],color=['#c9c6ac','#da9100'])
plt.axhline(2,color='#af983f',ls='--',lw=2,label='true=2'); plt.legend()
plt.title(f'gamma={{gamma}}:  OLS={ols:.2f}   2SLS={iv:.2f}')

stages.title: Check: what goes into the second stage?
stages.prompt: In 2SLS, the second-stage regression of y is run on…
choices: the raw endogenous x
the fitted values x̂ from regressing x on the instruments
the instrument z directly
the residuals from the first stage
stages.hint: We want the clean part of x that z explains.
stages.explain: The second stage uses x̂, the projection of x onto the instruments. Because x̂ is built only from exogenous z, it is uncorrelated with the confounder, giving a consistent β̂₁.

stages.title: Check: why not hand-roll the SEs?
stages.prompt: Why prefer IV2SLS over manually running sm.OLS(y, x̂) for the second stage?
choices: The manual coefficient is biased
The manual standard errors are wrong because they ignore that x̂ is estimated
IV2SLS uses a different, larger sample
There is no difference at all
stages.hint: The point estimate matches; something else does not.
stages.explain: Both give the same β̂₁, but plugging x̂ into a naive OLS understates uncertainty because it treats the generated regressor as if it were observed. IV2SLS corrects the variance.

stages.title: The clean slice of x
stages.lead: 2SLS runs in two moves: regress x on the instruments, keep the predictions, then run the structural equation on those.
stages.prompt: In 2SLS the second stage regresses y not on the raw endogenous x, but on the ___ values x̂ that the first stage predicts from the instruments.
stages.hint: It's the part of x that z explains — the clean, exogenous slice, written x̂.
stages.explain: The blank is fitted (predicted) values, x̂. The misconception this defuses is 'plug the instrument z straight into the second stage' — you regress y on x̂, not on z and not on the first-stage residuals. x̂ keeps only the variation in x that z explains, stripping out the confounded part. Boundary: with one instrument and one endogenous regressor this two-stage fit numerically equals the simple IV ratio Cov(z,y)/Cov(z,x); with extra instruments it does not, which is the over-identified case.

stages.title: Hand-rolled second-stage SEs
stages.prompt: Claim: running the second stage by hand with sm.OLS(y, x̂) gives both the right 2SLS coefficient and the right standard errors.
stages.hint: The point estimate matches; think about what x̂ being estimated (not observed) does to the uncertainty.
stages.explain: This is the manual-2SLS-is-fine trap. The hand-rolled coefficient is correct, but the standard errors are wrong: sm.OLS(y, x̂) treats x̂ as if it were observed data, ignoring that x̂ was itself estimated in the first stage, so it understates the true sampling variability. Use a dedicated IV2SLS estimator, which corrects the SEs. Boundary: the bias is only in the inference (SEs, t-stats, CIs) — the β̂ from the manual route is identical, so the fix is the SE formula, not the point estimate.

modules.title: 4 · Diagnostics
modules.summary: First-stage F flags weak instruments; over-identification tests probe exclusion.

stages.title: Weak instruments and the first-stage F
stages.html:
How strong is your instrument?

Relevance is not yes/no — it is a matter of degree. A weak instrument barely moves x, so Cov(z,x) is tiny and the IV ratio divides by near-zero. Consequences:

  • 2SLS standard errors balloon — estimates become wildly imprecise.
  • Worse, weak instruments reintroduce bias toward OLS in finite samples, and the usual SEs understate the true uncertainty.

The standard diagnostic is the first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instruments — from sm.OLS(x, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fvalue. A common rule of thumb (Staiger–Stock):

first-stage F ≳ 10 → instrument is "strong enough"

Key idea. Always report the first-stage F. An F in the low single digits is a red flag: your 2SLS results may be unreliable no matter how clean the exclusion story is.

stages.title: Over-identification: a partial check on exclusion
stages.html:
When you have spare instruments

If you have more valid instruments than endogenous regressors, the model is over-identified. Each instrument gives its own estimate of β₁; if all instruments are valid, those estimates should agree (up to sampling noise). An over-identification test (Sargan / Hansen J) checks exactly this.

The intuition: take the 2SLS residuals and regress them on all the instruments. Under a valid set, the instruments should have no explanatory power for the residual, so

J = n·R² ~ χ²(#instruments − #endogenous)

A small J / large p-value is consistent with valid instruments; a small p-value says at least one instrument fails exclusion (or the model is misspecified).

Key idea. Over-ID tests can only reject validity — passing is reassuring but not proof, and the test is silent in the just-identified case (one instrument, one endogenous regressor), where there is nothing to compare against.

stages.title: Weak vs strong: F and 2SLS side by side
stages.note: Same structure, only the instrument's strength changes. Watch the first-stage F and the 2SLS estimate/SE move together.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000

def run(pi):
    u = rng.normal(0,1,n); z = rng.normal(0,1,n)
    x = pi*z + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
    y = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)   # true beta1 = 2
    F  = sm.OLS(x, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fvalue
    iv = IV2SLS(y, sm.add_constant(x), sm.add_constant(z)).fit()
    return F, iv.params[1], iv.bse[1]

print(f"{'pi':>5}{'first-F':>10}{'2SLS b1':>10}{'SE':>8}")
pis=[0.05,0.1,0.3,0.8,1.5]; Fs=[]; bs=[]
for pi in pis:
    F,b,se=run(pi); Fs.append(F); bs.append(b)
    tag='  <-- weak (F<10)' if F<10 else ''
    print(f'{pi:5.2f}{F:10.1f}{b:10.2f}{se:8.2f}{tag}')

fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.7))
ax[0].plot(pis,Fs,'o-',color='#da9100',lw=2); ax[0].axhline(10,color='#c9c6ac',ls='--')
ax[0].set_title('first-stage F'); ax[0].set_xlabel('pi')
ax[1].plot(pis,bs,'o-',color='#af983f',lw=2); ax[1].axhline(2,color='#c9c6ac',ls='--')
ax[1].set_title('2SLS beta1_hat'); ax[1].set_xlabel('pi')
fig.tight_layout()

stages.title: Weak-instrument slider
stages.note: Drag π. The title shows the first-stage F and the 2SLS estimate. Below ~10 the estimate jumps around and the SE explodes — the weak-instrument danger zone.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000
u=rng.normal(0,1,n); z=rng.normal(0,1,n)
x={{pi}}*z+1.0*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
y=1+2*x+3*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
F=sm.OLS(x,sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fvalue
iv=IV2SLS(y,sm.add_constant(x),sm.add_constant(z)).fit()
b,se=iv.params[1],iv.bse[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.errorbar([0],[b],yerr=[1.96*se],fmt='o',color='#da9100',capsize=8,ms=10,label='2SLS 95% CI')
plt.axhline(2,color='#af983f',ls='--',lw=2,label='true=2')
plt.xlim(-1,1); plt.xticks([]); plt.legend()
weak=' WEAK' if F<10 else ' strong'
plt.title(f'F={F:.1f}{weak}   2SLS b1={b:.2f}  SE={se:.2f}')

stages.title: Over-identification (Sargan) intuition
stages.note: Two instruments, one endogenous x. We compute the Sargan J statistic by regressing 2SLS residuals on the instruments. Valid instruments → large p-value; an instrument that leaks into y → tiny p-value.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(3); n=1000
u  = rng.normal(0,1,n)
z1 = rng.normal(0,1,n); z2 = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x  = 0.8*z1 + 0.7*z2 + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y  = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)       # both instruments excluded -> valid

exog  = sm.add_constant(x)
instr = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z1, z2])
iv = IV2SLS(y, exog, instr).fit()
print('2SLS beta1_hat =', round(iv.params[1],3), ' (true 2)')

# Sargan J: regress 2SLS residuals on ALL instruments; J = n*R^2 ~ chi2(#instr - #endog)
resid = y - exog @ iv.params
aux = sm.OLS(resid, instr).fit()
J = n * aux.rsquared
dof = instr.shape[1] - exog.shape[1]   # 3 instrument cols - 2 exog cols = 1
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(J, dof)
print(f'Sargan J = {J:.3f}  dof={dof}  p-value = {p:.3f}')
print('large p-value -> no evidence against instrument validity (good)')

# Now BREAK exclusion: let z2 leak directly into y
y_bad = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + 1.5*z2 + rng.normal(0,1,n)
iv_b = IV2SLS(y_bad, exog, instr).fit()
resid_b = y_bad - exog @ iv_b.params
J_b = n * sm.OLS(resid_b, instr).fit().rsquared
p_b = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(J_b, dof)
print(f'\nwith z2 invalid:  J = {J_b:.2f}  p-value = {p_b:.3f}  -> test REJECTS validity')

stages.title: Check: reading the first-stage F
stages.prompt: Your first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instrument is 2.3. What is the appropriate concern?
choices: The exclusion restriction is violated
The instrument is weak; 2SLS may be biased and very imprecise
The model is over-identified
Nothing — any positive F is fine
stages.hint: Compare against the rule-of-thumb threshold of about 10.
stages.explain: An F well below 10 signals a weak instrument: the first stage barely moves x, so 2SLS estimates are imprecise and biased toward OLS, with unreliable standard errors.

stages.title: Check: the over-ID test
stages.prompt: With two instruments and one endogenous regressor, the Sargan/Hansen J test returns a very small p-value. This suggests…
choices: the instruments are strong
at least one instrument likely violates the exclusion restriction
the first stage is weak
β₁ is exactly 2
stages.hint: The test compares the estimates implied by different instruments.
stages.explain: A small p-value rejects the null that all instruments are valid: the over-identifying instruments disagree, pointing to an exclusion violation (or misspecification). It cannot run in the just-identified case.

stages.title: First-stage F vs the rule of thumb
stages.prompt: The first stage regresses x on the excluded instrument; the F-statistic on that instrument is 6.4. Using the Staiger–Stock rule of thumb (F ≈ 10), how far above or below the threshold are you? Enter a signed number (e.g. −3.6).
stages.hint: Subtract the threshold from your F: 6.4 − 10.
stages.explain: 6.4 − 10 = −3.6, i.e. 3.6 below the rule-of-thumb 10 — a weak instrument. This is the significance≠strength trap again in numbers: that same first stage could have a significant t-stat, yet an F of 6.4 means 2SLS is biased toward OLS with distorted standard errors. 'Significant' and 'strong' are different claims; only the F speaks to strength. Boundary: F ≳ 10 is a rough threshold, not a bright line — values just above it are reassuring, low single digits are a clear red flag regardless of how clean the exclusion story is.

stages.title: What a passed over-ID test proves
stages.prompt: Your over-identified model has 3 instruments for 1 endogenous regressor. The Sargan/Hansen J test returns a large p-value (you fail to reject). What can you correctly conclude?
choices: The exclusion restriction is now proven — all 3 instruments are valid
The result is consistent with valid instruments, but exclusion remains an untested assumption
At least one instrument violates exclusion
The instruments are strong (high first-stage F)
why: The over-ID test can only reject; a non-rejection never proves validity.
That is what a SMALL p-value (rejection) would suggest, not a large one.
The J test checks exclusion/over-ID agreement, not strength — strength is the first-stage F.
stages.hint: The J test can only ever reject validity; ask what failing to reject does and doesn't establish.
stages.explain: This is the passed-test-proves-exogeneity trap. The over-ID (Sargan/Hansen J) test can only reject validity: a large p-value is consistent with valid instruments but proves nothing — the test has low power and must assume at least one instrument is valid to anchor on. Exclusion/exogeneity stays an argument you defend, not a result you read off. The strength distractor confuses two diagnostics: weakness is the first-stage F, validity is the J test. Boundary: the J test is also silent when the model is just-identified (one instrument, one regressor) — there are no spare instruments to disagree, so there is nothing to test.
